plan.topic: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) vs semaglutide (Wegovy) in the only randomized head-to-head obesity trial, SURMOUNT-5 (NEJM 2025): adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition, without diabetes; 72 weeks; open-label; Lilly-funded; each drug at the maximum tolerated dose.
plan.angle: Keep the plan as written, with these changes. Replace 'the only randomized head-to-head obesity trial' with 'the first big randomized trial to compare them directly', or simply 'the trial that randomly assigned people to one or the other'. Use no 'only', 'first ever' or 'new' wording elsewhere either. Sentence 1 example: 'In adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without type 2 diabetes, who lost more weight: tirzepatide or semaglutide, in the trial that randomly assigned people to one or the other?' Copy every per-arm number from the NEJM paper on PubMed (PMID 40353578), and name the measure (average percent change at 72 weeks), both arms, the population and 'open-label, Lilly-funded, maximum tolerated doses'. The thumbnail keeps 'WHO LOST MORE?' with 'Tirzepatide vs semaglutide' as subtext. Chapter 6 gives one neutral line per separate trial, with no ranking and no approval claims beyond Section 1 of each US label.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide (Zepbound) vs Wegovy: Who Lost More?
plan.why: This is an approved-drug head-to-head search format like our top earner, EloraTZP. It's broad enough to be suggested, it rests on one peer-reviewed RCT so it's easy to verify, and pill-launch comparison searches are rising again. | fact-check: The core facts check out against an independent summary of the NEJM paper (ACC Journal Scan, 10 Jul 2025). SURMOUNT-5 was a Phase 3b, open-label trial with 1:1 randomization and 751 participants at 32 US and Puerto Rico sites. Participants were adults with BMI ≥30, or ≥27 plus at least one obesity-related complication, without type 2 diabetes. It ran 72 weeks. Each drug was given at its maximum tolerated dose: tirzepatide 10 or 15 mg, semaglutide 1.7 or 2.4 mg. Results: −20.2% vs −13.7% body weight, about 22.8 kg vs 15.0 kg. Weill Cornell confirms Dr. Aronne led it and Lilly's release confirms Lilly funded it. The angle is well hedged: averages not predictions, side effects not formally compared, separate trials not ranked, no titration, cost or switching talk, boxed MTC or MEN 2 line, and the prescriber line. Long-form allows a subscribe ask and a 'linked in the description' ending, so neither is a problem. Changes needed: (1) 'The only randomized head-to-head obesity trial' is an absolute claim we can't verify, and it will go out of date once new trials report, which breaks the evergreen rule. Sources describe it as the 'first' head-to-head. (2) The scriptwriter must check per-arm figures (≥25% threshold shares, waist change, GI rates and GI-related stopping) against the NEJM abstract or tables on PubMed, not news summaries. They must also confirm which estimand gives −20.2/−13.7 before tagging it 'counting everyone who started'. If the paper's primary figures turn out to be the efficacy estimand, use the paper's exact treatment-regimen numbers instead. (3) The −20.2/−13.7 figures are least-squares means. Say 'average' without suggesting it is a typical person's result. (4) Chapter 6 must not suggest that semaglutide 7.2 mg or oral GLP-1s are approved for weight loss beyond what each US label says. Give trial names only, with no comparison. (5) Before production, check the live list for an existing SURMOUNT-5 long video (10-15) and flag any duplicate to the owner.

package.description:
This trial doesn't tell you to switch medicines. Switching between tirzepatide and semaglutide is a decision for you and your prescriber. Not personal advice.

Quick answer: In SURMOUNT-5, adults with obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, without type 2 diabetes were randomly assigned to tirzepatide or semaglutide, each at the maximum tolerated dose. At 72 weeks, tirzepatide averaged 20.2% weight loss vs 13.7% for semaglutide. Open-label, Lilly-funded (NEJM, 2025).

factcheck.summary:
I checked every number and study description against the primary records: the SURMOUNT-5 abstract (via Europe PMC, the same text as PubMed 40353578), the ClinicalTrials.gov record NCT05822830, the Zepbound label on DailyMed (revised 28 Aug 2026), and the SURMOUNT-1, STEP 1, SURMOUNT-OSA and SELECT abstracts. Everything matches its source:
- SURMOUNT-5 was phase 3b, open-label and funded by Eli Lilly, with 751 adults randomized 1:1.
- Each arm used its maximum tolerated dose: tirzepatide 10 or 15 mg, semaglutide 1.7 or 2.4 mg, for 72 weeks.
- Average weight change was −20.2% (95% CI −21.4 to −19.1) on tirzepatide vs −13.7% (95% CI −14.9 to −12.6) on semaglutide. The ranges really don't overlap.
- Average waist change was −18.4 vs −13.0 cm.
- Tirzepatide was ahead at all four milestones (10%, 15%, 20% and 25%).
- The most common adverse events in both groups were gastrointestinal, mostly mild to moderate and mainly during dose escalation.
- The s20 conclusion is quoted word for word.
- Eligibility was BMI 30 or more, or 27 or more with a weight-related condition, and diabetes was excluded.
- The label's two uses (weight, including sleep apnea), its mechanism and its MTC/MEN 2 boxed warning are stated correctly.
- The pancreatitis line keeps "with or without vomiting" and "right away", followed by the scoped don't-stop line.
- The other four trials are each described as one drug vs placebo, with the right population and length, and the script never lines up numbers across separate trials.
- The 220 lb and inch conversions are correct and clearly labelled as illustrations.
- Priya is clearly a hypothetical.
- The open-label design and Lilly funding are disclosed, and the "talk to your doctor or prescriber" line is in s69.

I found no major problems. The issues below are small wording fixes for accuracy and the muted-viewer test.

issues.claim: That's a gap of six and a half percentage points, measured at seventy-two weeks, in the paper's main result.
issues.problem: The abstract gives the two averages, not a 6.5-point difference. The 6.5 is our own subtraction, and "in the paper's main result" makes it sound quoted.
issues.fix: That's a gap of about six and a half percentage points between the two averages at seventy-two weeks, the trial's main measure.

issues.claim: With obesity and no type two diabetes, she'd meet the main entry rules.
issues.problem: The script never says Priya has obesity, and the trial excluded diabetes of any type ("Diabetes mellitus"), not just type 2. Making the sentence conditional keeps it accurate.
issues.fix: If she has obesity, or overweight plus a weight-related condition, and no diabetes, she'd meet the main entry rules. If she had type two diabetes, this trial didn't include people like her.

issues.claim: One sign never waits ... For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
issues.problem: The scene names one sign but then says "those emergency signs" (plural). Keep the required don't-stop line word for word and change only the opener.
issues.fix: Some signs never wait. Severe pain in your stomach area that won't go away, with or without vomiting, is one. If that happens, stop using the medicine and call your healthcare provider right away. For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.

issues.claim: adults forty-five and older with heart disease and overweight or obesity
issues.problem: SELECT enrolled people with "preexisting cardiovascular disease" and a BMI of 27 or more. That includes stroke and peripheral artery disease, not only heart disease. The endpoint parts were nonfatal heart attack and nonfatal stroke.
issues.fix: SELECT tested semaglutide against placebo in adults forty-five and older with established cardiovascular disease and overweight or obesity, without diabetes, and found a lower risk of a combined outcome: cardiovascular death, nonfatal heart attack or nonfatal stroke.

issues.claim: side effects weren't this trial's main question
issues.problem: The source uses "adverse events", and our rule is never to swap that for "side effects" when describing trial data.
issues.fix: One honest caveat: adverse events weren't this trial's main question. Weight was. So read the safety results as a description, not a ranking of which drug is gentler.

Most SFX already sit nicely in the -14 to -20dB felt zone; I trimmed about twenty outlier cues (several swooshes/pops/blips landing between -5 and -11dB under active narration, e.g. around 8-11s, 42s, 86-89s, 201s, 264s, 286s, 413-414s, 458s and 583s) back down to roughly -16dB so nothing peeks over the words. Left the many heavily-ducked swells/ticks (often -30 to -55dB) alone since they occur under dense speech and are correctly staying out of the way. Added five bespoke, medical-safety-clean accents (chime/piano/marimba/bell) at the stat reveal, the Priya story turn, the "severe stomach pain" caution line, the boxed-warning heading and the closing "watch this next" button, each kept subtle to match the mood of its beat.

thumbnail.reasoning: Candidate #0 is disqualified on two counts: the headline is literally clipped by the TRIAL badge (reads 'HO LOST MORE?' even at full size), and the red X / green check icons on the two mascots visually telegraph which drug 'lost' — this gives away the answer and also closely echoes the title's own wording, so it's capped low on both legibility and CTR despite a clean versus layout. Candidates #1 and #2 are both clean, legible, and preserve the curiosity gap without revealing the result. #2 ('HOW BIG A GAP?') pairs its headline more tightly with a strong, on-theme visual metaphor (the scale, tied directly to a 'comparison/weight' concept) and a genuinely shocked expression, giving it a slightly stronger emotional pull and focal point than the big-number treatment in #1, while both are fully legible at phone size. #2 is the best pick with legibility well above the 7 threshold and the highest estimated CTR among safe, non-misleading options.
